article.title: Build Live Apps in Cursor · Cursor
article.text:
Nov 5, 2026 · Changelog
Changelog
Build Live Apps in Cursor
Agents have lowered the cost of writing code, but most apps and tools that users build never make it off of localhost.
Now, you can build live apps directly in Cursor and share them with a link. Describe what you want to create and Cursor will handle the rest: build the app, set up a database, configure auth, and deploy it.
With this release, anyone in your org can now build useful tools for their work and share them with teammates. Update Cursor to try it out.
#How it works
To get started, kick off a cloud agent and tell it explicitly that you want to build an app.
Cursor will scaffold the web app, spin up a Postgres database if needed, set up authentication behind Cursor SSO, and provision hosting. If the app needs to connect to your systems, like a data warehouse, Cursor will ask for the secrets it needs.
When you go to publish your app, you pick a unique domain and Cursor gets you back a live link.
At Cursor, users across sales, operations, legal, finance, and engineering are building internal apps. Some of the most useful ones are:
Internal ops tools for event registration, account assignments, and desk seating
Multimedia presentations for customers that combine slides, videos, and interactive demos
Training, enablement, and onboarding experiences for new hires
Live dashboards and tools for sales teams to understand their pipeline and opportunities
Portals to manage engineering services
Cursor can deploy apps from new or existing repos across Cursor Origin and GitHub. Support for other git providers like GitLab is coming soon.
#Controls and guardrails
When you publish an app, Cursor will run deterministic and agentic security checks to catch common issues, like secrets written in app files or exposed credentials. If a check fails, the agent tells you what it needs to fix. Nothing goes live until the checks pass and you explicitly publish the app.
Team admins can see every app and secret on the team. They can also add their own rules to the security review, approve publishes the review blocked, and unpublish any app.
#Share with your team
Once the checks pass, Cursor deploys the app to the URL you chose. You can then share your app with specific people, groups, or your entire team, all behind Cursor sign-in. On individual plans, you can also share apps publicly.
You can also provision a Cursor API key if you want a script or Grok Bot to use your app.
#Get started
This capability is now available on all paid plans with cloud agents enabled. Learn more by reading our docs.

hn.title: Launch HN: Rivet (YC W23) – Scale and Orchestrate Agents on S3
hn.text:
Hey HN, this is Nathan and Nicholas from Rivet (https://rivet.dev) – a fast, high-density, and scalable orchestrator for agentic workloads using the actor model. Rather than running a heavyweight sandbox per agent, each agent gets a lightweight actor backed by S3.
Actors provide a long-lived process for long agent turns, in-memory state for context, a WebSocket server for multiplayer, durable SQLite storage backed by S3, and hibernation when idle.
It's a similar model to Cloudflare Durable Objects, but it’s open source and self-hostable.
Here’s a video walkthrough: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3Ev6I7DOV9c
When we went through YC in 2023, we were building infrastructure for multiplayer games like Diep and Krunker. This involved heavily optimizing high-throughput matchmaking, real-time player messages, and blitz scaling. Through that process, we spent a lot of time on workloads where Postgres couldn't keep up with our throughput. We started out by hacking together Lua scripts on top of Redis, but this became too cumbersome to maintain and upgrade. This led us to extend our game server orchestrator to support what we call Rivet Actors today: many lightweight workers with in-memory state and durable storage. By using actors, we were able to serve tens of millions of monthly active users.
As agents grew in popularity, it became clear that running agents in sandboxes is inefficient. Sandboxes are expensive, mostly idle, and slow to start. Developers started using actors because they are far more memory efficient (72 KB baseline for actors vs 512 MB for a minimal sandbox) and fast to start (4.9 ms p99 for actors vs 1.7 s p99 for sandboxes).
For example, Amp is using Rivet to orchestrate multiplayer agents. They originally tried to build on Cloudflare Durable Objects, but couldn’t launch because of the platform’s limitations and unresponsive support. They migrated to Rivet Actors in a weekend and deploy on-prem. Rivet’s flexible architecture lets them adapt it to their own use cases without being constrained by a framework or the memory, storage, and runtime limits of Cloudflare Durable Objects.
Under the hood, Rivet is backed by S3 while maintaining SSD speeds.
Why S3? Previously, Rivet ran on FoundationDB. However, we were surprised to find that companies are storing orders of magnitude more data on Rivet Actors than in Postgres, such as large session transcripts, agent artifacts, and full POSIX filesystems. As their data grew, they had to start paying for SSDs that sat mostly idle with old transcripts. This led us to double down on S3 as our primary storage medium without sacrificing performance. This choice means that data stored on Rivet is 10× cheaper than on EBS gp3 while maintaining SSD speeds.
It’s not as simple as writing data straight to S3. Lots of PUTs for tiny blobs of data are slow and expensive. Instead, we use an SSD tier to optimize speed and cost:
When you write data to an actor’s SQLite database, the write is acknowledged once SSDs in 2 of 3 availability zones have it. Then, the data is batched to S3 in the background. This means that S3 is never on the write path, which lowers latency and cost. When reading data or waking an actor, Rivet reads from SSDs if already cached and falls back to S3 if not. SSD caches can be tuned to meet your needs, giving you configurable tiered storage for your actors.
This architecture lets Rivet provide 1.07 ms durable writes (3 AZ, p99), 1.36 ms reads (p99), and 138 ms reads from object storage (p99).
We’ve spent a lot of time making sure that Rivet can run wherever you need it. Self-hosting requires deploying a single Rust binary with S3 as the only dependency, Rivet Cloud lets you deploy dedicated clusters on AWS or GCP in any region, and BYOC lets us deploy Rivet to your VPC without having to operate it yourself. Rivet also runs identically in local dev as in production, since Rivet is a lightweight binary that runs anywhere
Rivet Actors can be written in TypeScript or Rust.…

hn.title: Ask HN: What's your current AI agentic setup?
hn.text:
I'm curious how people on HN are using AI day to day, and came up with a list of questions I thought could be interesting to know. No need to answer every question of course, just wanted to get a gut feel how people are using AI.
1) What AI subscriptions are you personally paying for? (Claude, ChatGPT/Codex, Cursor, etc)
- Which tiers?
- Have you purchased multiple subscriptions from the same provider (eg two Claude accounts)?
2) Are you using models outside (or instead) of those subscriptions? For example, pay-as-you-go APIs, OpenRouter, or locally hosted models.
- Which models and providers?
3) What coding harnesses and interfaces are you using? Are you sticking with the default CLIs or IDE integrations, or using alternatives like OpenCode, Pi, Aider, Muse Code, or custom-built harnesses?
- What made you switch harnesses (if you switched)?
4) Are you using any agent orchestration or swarm tools?
- For example, Munder Difflin, Gas Town, Ruflo, or something custom.
5) Are you using broader agent platforms like OpenClaw / Hermes Agent / Grok bot / Dots / Muse?
- If you are using them, what are your main use cases?
-----
I know my workflow has differed significantly from a year ago, and so it would be interesting to capture a snapshot today of what people are using and why.

article.text:
### Who is really in charge of your agent?
[](https://github.com/AGGIB/Stroq/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[](docs/GUIDE.md#replay-thirty-six-attacks-from-public-reports-and-synthetic-cells)
[](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@stroq/cli)
[](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@stroq/cli)
[](LICENSE)
Stroq reads your own Claude Code and Codex sessions and shows how many commands came from text your agent read, and which keys left your machine.
An example: a made-up machine with made-up sessions, keys and hosts. Hoo is Stroq's owl. Your card shows your own sessions.
```bash
npx @stroq/cli
```
It reads your last 30 days of sessions, your key files and the folders your agent worked in; prints key names, never values; writes nothing but a small cache under `~/.stroq`; and sends nothing. No account, no telemetry.
```text
npx @stroq/cli a card of your own sessions, like the one above
npx @stroq/cli init stop it next time: guard your agent
npx @stroq/cli why why an action was stopped
npx @stroq/cli attack watch Stroq stop 36 known attacks, in a sandbox
npx @stroq/cli uninstall remove Stroq
```
Every moment on the card has a `stroq show` line that prints the evidence behind it (`npx @stroq/cli show 1`). `stroq help --all` lists the other commands. Needs Node.js 22 or newer. Apache-2.0.
## Beyond the card
Stroq is a local security platform for AI coding agents: Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI and others. Its hooks judge every tool call before it runs. They deny `curl | sh` and outbound calls that carry a known secret from your machine, and they ask you first when a command repeats text the agent read, naming that text. The console shows which agents actually ask Stroq, and every decision with its reason. Sessions you already had can be checked too, without installing anything.
```bash
npx @stroq/cli console # the console: a private page on 127.0.0.1
npx @stroq/cli replay --all # your Claude Code sessions of the last 30 days against the policy; no hooks needed
npx @stroq/cli sent # did your agent pass your keys on? key names, never values
npx @stroq/cli init # hook into your agent and guard the next session
```
A made-up machine: made-up sessions, keys and hosts. Nothing was executed.
## The console
Check: the card of stroq, made by the same code. Each moment opens with its evidence, under it one line for each agent.
Live: recorded decisions as they happen. A row opens into its chain: what the agent read, what it did, the decision, the rule.
Agents: add or remove Stroq's hooks, with the exact file change shown first. When Stroq was last asked, and which of an agent's settings weaken it.
Skills & MCP: every skill and MCP server by agent: where it came from, what the rules matched in it, what changed since you last looked.
The fifth screen is **Rules**: try an action without running it, turn rules on with a preview and a test, the history with an undo, and the rules reference. Connected means Stroq's hooks are in the agent's settings, not that the agent calls them: **Test hook** and **Live** show that.
Screens from a build just before 0.30.0, reading a made-up machine: made-up sessions, keys and hosts. Nothing was executed.
```sh
npx @stroq/cli console # a private page on 127.0.0.1
npx @stroq/cli console --workspace /path/to/repo # the project it should look at
```
Open the whole link it prints: it carries a key that is new each time the console starts. The console reads what Stroq already records on this machine. It changes an agent's settings or Stroq's policy only after you confirm a preview of that change; checks you run are saved under `~/.stroq`.
It listens only on 127.0.0.1, needs no account and has no telemetry. Nothing in it starts your agent: **Test hook** runs the hook once, offline. Adding hooks from the console needs macOS or Linux; on Windows use `stroq init`. Details and limits: [console guide](console/README.md).
